arXiv:2610.20205v1 [cs.HC] 14 Oct 2026

What and Where in Identifying and Quantifying
Conventions in Humans and AI Agents

Makoto Fukushima Affiliation: Honda Research Institute Japan    Tim Puphal Affiliation: Honda Research Institute Europe
Abstract

Cooperative success rests in part on implicit communication. Partners converge on conventions: regularities that give an action meaning beyond its direct effect. Yet conventions are usually observed only indirectly: a score drop when partners are swapped shows that a convention existed, but not what it was or where it was used. In the card game Hanabi, the exact probability that a play fails can be computed from the hints received and the cards in view. Players who use conventions succeed more often than this prediction allows; the resulting margin is the convention gap. Off-belief learning provides a hierarchy of agents (levels 1–5) whose first level uses no conventions by construction and whose later levels use progressively more. For humans and these agents on one scale, we ask what the conventions are and where they are used. On what: in two independently collected corpora of human games, humans show a larger gap than every agent level. On the conventions both populations use, however, humans do no better than level 2. The human advantage is concentrated in a situation that no agent level learns to use: hints that point to a card other than the ones they touch. On where: conventions depend on what the player already knows about the card, not on how recently it was hinted, and they are used most in the mid-game; humans use them earlier and later in the game than the agents. In interventions on the agents, blocking a single high-gap situation costs little, because meaning reroutes to other situations, but blocking several together costs far more than the sum of the single costs. Thus, the convention gap turns conventions from an inferred cause of score loss into a measurable, comparable, and causally testable object.

1 Introduction

Successful cooperation depends in part on implicit communication. Partners converge on conventions: regularities that give an action a meaning beyond its direct effect (Lewis, 1969). People and AI agents both rely on conventions alongside the explicit information the rules provide. In zero-shot coordination (ZSC) (Hu et al., 2020; Treutlein et al., 2021), conventions are what break when a policy meets a partner it was not trained with. Yet conventions are usually studied indirectly, through the score an agent loses when its partner is swapped. A score drop shows that a convention existed. It does not say what the convention was, where it operated, what it was worth, or whether humans share it.

A recent study (Fukushima et al., 2026) proposes a more direct diagnostic in the cooperative card game Hanabi (Bard et al., 2020). At every play action, a literal observer computes the exact probability that the played card fails, using only information the rules guarantee: the hint constraints on every card in the hand, and card counting over all visible zones. Averaged over many plays, the difference between this predicted failure rate and the actual one is the convention gap (Fukushima et al., 2026). Off-belief learning (OBL) trains a hierarchy of agents (Hu et al., 2021). Level 1 is trained to read past actions only for their literal content, and later levels may interpret more. On this hierarchy, the gap rose monotonically with level, from +1.57+1.57 to +21.68+21.68 percentage points (pp) (Fukushima et al., 2026).

Here, we identify candidate conventions where plays beat the literal prediction, and quantify that departure in pp. We ask three questions of humans and the OBL hierarchy on one scale. (i) What are the conventions: which situations carry the gap, and to what extent do the two populations agree on them? (ii) Where are they used: when in the game, in which situations, and carried by which feature of the game state? (iii) To what extent does removing a convention cost score, relative to removing an equally frequent play at random? We address them by breaking the gap down by situation and by turn, by placing a public human corpus (Hanab Live, 2026) and a second, independently collected corpus (Dizdarević et al., 2025) on the same scale as the hierarchy, and by intervening on the agents’ policies against a frequency-matched control.

Findings in brief.

The convention gap of the human corpus, +26.16​[+24.05,+28.28]​pp+26.16~[+24.05,+28.28]\,\text{pp}, is larger than that of every level of the OBL hierarchy, and their profile across play situations replicates on the second corpus (r=0.97r=0.97; Appendix E). On the conventions both populations share, humans are not significantly closer to level 5 than to level 2. The remaining difference lies in one situation where no level approaches the human gap: hints that point to a card other than the one they touch (indirect reference; §3.1). The gap peaks in the mid-game, and the human gap exceeds level 5’s in the opening and late game. In the agents, the gap follows what the player already knows about the played card rather than how recently it was hinted (§3.2). Finally, blocking one high-gap situation in the agents’ play lowers their score little more than blocking an equally frequent play at random, because blocked plays partly reappear in other situations; blocking several situations together costs more than the sum of the single blocks (−1.84-1.84 points jointly against −0.77-0.77 summed; §3.3). Together, these results show how an exact literal baseline can locate and compare conventions across humans and agents, and price them in agents.

1.1 Related work

Conventions and zero-shot coordination.

A convention in Lewis’s sense is a self-sustaining regularity that resolves a coordination problem among alternatives (Lewis, 1969). In cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning such regularities are what self-play policies acquire, and the Hanabi challenge made their cost visible: policies that score well together fail with partners trained separately (Bard et al., 2020). The ZSC program addresses this by construction. Other-Play removes symmetry-dependent conventions (Hu et al., 2020); off-belief learning trains its first level to read past actions only for their literal content and lets later levels interpret more (Hu et al., 2021); K-level reasoning, trajectory diversity, and the label-free formalism of Treutlein et al. (2021) give further routes to compatible policies (Cui et al., 2021; Lupu et al., 2021). Evaluation in this line is by cross-play score (Wolski et al., 2026). This paper proposes no ZSC method; it locates the conventions those methods act on, using the off-belief learning hierarchy.

Human–AI coordination and human proxies.

Evaluating agents with people is costly, so the field increasingly substitutes behavioral clones of human play. The practice was established in Overcooked (Carroll et al., 2019); population-based training aims to remove the need for human data altogether (Strouse et al., 2021); in Hanabi, human-team studies (Siu et al., 2021) and the AH2AC2 benchmark, whose proxies are cloned from human games (Dizdarević et al., 2025), follow the same route. Appendix H tests what such clones preserve at the level of individual conventions.

Reading conventions out of policies.

Shih et al. (2021) separate a policy into a task-specific module and a partner-specific convention module and show that the latter transfers across tasks; Any-Play augments training to discourage conventions (Lucas and Allen, 2022). Both treat conventions as a hidden variable to be separated out or suppressed. Here plays are compared with an exact literal baseline, so a convention’s location and carrier can be reported without a learned probe.

Implicit communication and pragmatics.

Hints in Hanabi are speech acts whose intended meaning exceeds their literal content, the situation the rational speech act framework models as recursive inference between speaker and listener (Frank and Goodman, 2012; Goodman and Frank, 2016), building on Gricean implicature and common ground (Grice, 1975; Clark, 1996). The convention gap needs no fitted listener: it compares observed failures with literal predictions, in percentage points of failure.

Depth of reasoning.

Level-kk and cognitive-hierarchy models estimate how many steps of recursive reasoning people use, and typically find one to three (Stahl and Wilson, 1995; Nagel, 1995; Camerer et al., 2004). Appendix F asks whether the human–agent difference is a difference of depth in that sense, and finds that depth alone does not account for it.

2 Methods

2.1 The convention gap

We use the metric as defined in a previous study (Fukushima et al., 2026). At every play action, an exact literal observer computes P⁡(life loss)P(\text{life loss}) from rule-guaranteed information only: the positive and negative hint constraints on every card in the hand, and card counting over all visible zones. Because a hint on one card also constrains the others, the observer uses the joint distribution over the whole hand rather than per-card marginals. For a set of plays,

Δ=mean⁡(P⁡(life loss))−actual life-loss rate,\Delta\;=\;\operatorname{mean}\big(P(\text{life loss})\big)\;-\;\text{actual life-loss rate}, (1)

reported in percentage points. A positive value means plays fail less often than literal information predicts. The gap is signed and cannot exceed the mean P⁡(life loss)P(\text{life loss}). It is exactly zero on plays whose outcome literal information fixes, and subsets with gaps of opposite sign can cancel. A value near zero therefore does not show that partners conveyed nothing beyond literal content. By quantifying conventions we mean locating where plays depart from this literal prediction and by how many percentage points. That a positive gap reflects conventions is an interpretation, not a definition: a partner who hints playable cards also produces one. The interpretation is consistent with the level ordering of §2.2 and the decompositions of §3.1–§3.3.

Statistics.

Each outcome is 00 or 11, so Δ\Delta is always a mean over many plays. Plays within a game share a deck and a history, so all intervals resample whole games (whole pairs, for humans) rather than individual plays (Cameron et al., 2008). Draw counts are fixed in advance. Where many data-induced categories (§2.4) are tested we control the false discovery rate at q=0.05q=0.05 per level (Benjamini and Hochberg, 1995). Wherever categories are induced from data, they are defined on a discovery half and every reported statistic is computed on a held-out estimation half, so no pattern is scored on the data that found it. Analyses with pre-specified categories use all plays.

2.2 The OBL hierarchy

Off-belief learning (Hu et al., 2021) trains a policy whose QQ-targets are computed on fictitious states, resampled from a belief model that assumes all past actions came from a fixed base policy π0\pi_{0}. The learner is scored as if the past carried only what π0\pi_{0} would put into it. Level 1 uses a uniformly random π0\pi_{0}, so it is trained to read past actions only for their literal content (grounded play). Each later level is trained with beliefs induced by the previous level’s policy, so it may interpret more. Agent levels are written level kk in the text and OBLkk in figures and tables. The released archive holds five seed models per level; the ladder below uses the first of each. Level 5 is in the archive but not among the results published with OBL (Hu et al., 2021), and every trend claim here holds on levels 1–4 alone. In the previous study (Fukushima et al., 2026), the gap rose monotonically with level, from +1.57​[+1.33,+1.81]​pp+1.57~[+1.33,+1.81]\,\text{pp} at level 1 to +21.68​[+21.34,+22.02]​pp+21.68~[+21.34,+22.02]\,\text{pp} at level 5. Level-1 cross-play, pooled over all pairings among five independently trained level-1 models, gave +1.22​[+0.98,+1.45]​pp+1.22~[+0.98,+1.45]\,\text{pp}.

Agent data.

Unless stated otherwise, agent conditions use 10001000 games per condition with distinct environment seeds and greedy acting; the taxonomy below pools five seed models per level (50005000 games; level 1 uses only the first).

2.3 Human data

People who play Hanabi competitively have conventions too, but theirs are taught: a player community publishes and teaches a convention system (H-Group, 2026). The human games are public logs from the hanab.live platform (Hanab Live, 2026), where this community plays. We first establish that these logs and the generated agent games are comparable. First, the same exact joint posterior is applied to both populations; nothing is re-estimated for humans. Second, the human games were replayed through the same extraction pipeline used for the agents and reproduced the reference posteriors bit-identically over all 90179017 plays. Third, the corpus and its filters are inherited unchanged from the previous study (Fukushima et al., 2026): a completed-games filter and a two-tier bot exclusion applied by the same code, giving 425425 games, 90179017 plays and 155155 players. Pairs recur across games (9595 pairs in all), so every human interval is clustered at the pair level. A second, independently collected corpus, the open games of the AH2AC2 benchmark (Dizdarević et al., 2025), is processed through the identical pipeline and serves as a replication corpus.

2.4 Situations and the induced taxonomy

Because Δ\Delta is a mean over plays, it can be broken down by situation. Two category systems do this. The first is hand-crafted: five mutually exclusive play situations (played immediately after a partner color hint touched the card; immediately after a rank hint; hinted earlier; unhinted and newest-drawn; unhinted and older). A card is unhinted if no hint has touched it; hints to other cards can still exclude values for it. Table 1 and §3.2 report the gap by situation. Plays made immediately after a hint touched a different card, indirect reference, are tracked with the finer categories described next.

The second system is induced from the data. Every play is described by six components of its context: the partner’s immediately preceding action, its relation to the board, the card’s ordered hint history, the lag since the last hint that touched it, hand position, and the hint-token stock. Games are split 50/50 into discovery and estimation halves. Every context type that clears a minimum cell size nminn_{\min} on the discovery half becomes its own category, and rarer types merge by hierarchical backoff, so there is no opaque other bucket. nminn_{\min} is derived from the empirical residual standard deviation at a ±5​pp\pm 5\,\text{pp} precision target, giving 52–139 across levels. A depth-4 CART tree (Breiman et al., 1984) fit on the same discovery half gives a compact summary of each taxonomy (Appendix A). All reported statistics come from the estimation half. The level-5 categories, once fit, are also kept fixed and applied unchanged to other populations; we call this the frozen level-5 taxonomy.

For comparing populations, a shared taxonomy is defined jointly on all six: a cell exists only if every population’s discovery half supports it at its own nminn_{\min}, so every value can be estimated for everyone. Each cell is labeled by the components that define it; Fig. 1 gives the key. We call any situation or category with a positive gap a channel.

2.5 Interventions

Categories are observational: a category’s gap says how far its plays depart from the literal prediction, not what would happen if the channel were removed. We therefore intervene on the agents’ policies. When the acting player’s greedy action is to play a card whose context falls in a target category, that play is removed from the legal set and the best remaining action is taken from the same network outputs. The network is not re-run, and its recurrent state follows the real observations. All conditions share 10001000 environment seeds, so scores are compared per deck. Verification gates precede every full run (Appendix D). Every score difference reported in §3.3 is therefore between the same decks and the same network.

The key part of the design is its control. Blocking any frequent play disturbs the game whatever its convention content, so a raw score drop says nothing about conventions. We therefore run frequency-matched random masks: the greedy play is blocked with a probability chosen to match a target category’s trigger rate, with no regard to its content, and these masks define a null cost curve. The quantity of interest is the excess cost: the paired score cost minus the random-mask cost at the same trigger rate, with the control curve re-fit inside every bootstrap draw. Three low-gap control categories at level 5 (two fully-identified-card cells and the large lag-4+4{+} rank cell) check the control curve (§3.3). Negative score changes are losses.

3 Results

3.1 What conventions are used: humans and agents on one scale

3.1.1 Humans sit above the OBL hierarchy, by a small, structured margin

How far above the OBL hierarchy does human play sit? The human corpus has a gap of +26.16​[+24.05,+28.28]​pp+26.16~[+24.05,+28.28]\,\text{pp}, against level 5’s +21.68​[+21.34,+22.02]​pp+21.68~[+21.34,+22.02]\,\text{pp} (Fig. 1, top row; mean ±\pm SD over the five seed models: +21.11±1.53​pp+21.11\pm 1.53\,\text{pp}, Appendix C). Humans are therefore above every level of the hierarchy (level-by-level view and bot-exclusion sensitivity: Appendix E).

The aggregate difference is mostly agreement.

Is the human margin spread across all situations, or concentrated in a few? Measured cell by cell on the shared taxonomy (§2.4; Fig. 1), it is concentrated. On the cells both populations share, the mean per-cell distance DkD_{k} between the human profile and the profile of level kk falls from D1=15.9D_{1}=15.9 to D2=4.1​ppD_{2}=4.1\,\text{pp}. On these cells, humans are not significantly closer to level 5 than to level 2 (D2−D5=+2.4​[−0.6,+3.5]​ppD_{2}-D_{5}=+2.4~[-0.6,+3.5]\,\text{pp}; Fig. 2). (Including the 1111 cells where the human value exceeds every level’s, the distance keeps falling slightly; Appendix F.) What remains of the human margin sits in a few rare cells: ranking the cells by the human–level-5 difference puts the two indirect-reference cells and a delayed color cell at the top (Appendix Fig. 9).

A Kitagawa–Oaxaca–Blinder split (Kitagawa, 1955; Oaxaca, 1973; Blinder, 1973) of the shared-cell difference (+25.81+25.81 against +21.12​pp+21.12\,\text{pp}, aggregates over the 2121 shared cells on the estimation halves) assigns +5.73​pp+5.73\,\text{pp} to gap differences within cells, weighted by human shares, and −1.03​pp-1.03\,\text{pp} to differences in cell shares, weighted by level-5 gaps. The split is an accounting identity. With the ranking above, the two populations are similar on everything frequent and differ in kind in a small family of rare situations.

The gap is not skill.

Could the human margin simply reflect stronger play? Level 5 outscores the average human game (24.1624.16 against the corpus mean of 18.5218.52), while humans have the larger gap. The gap says how far plays depart from their literal prediction, not how high a player scores. Two score-selected corpora point the same way. The AH2AC2 corpus, whose selection rule puts its mean score (23.4523.45) close to level 5’s, has a gap of +27.62​[+27.27,+27.97]​pp+27.62~[+27.27,+27.97]\,\text{pp}, and hanab.live games above the same score floor give +27.20​[+26.29,+28.04]​pp+27.20~[+26.29,+28.04]\,\text{pp} (Appendix E). Both select on final score, and so on failed plays, so they describe these games rather than control for skill. Because the platform’s community publishes and teaches a convention system, the estimate describes taught play, not typical human play.

3.1.2 The human profile replicates on an independently collected corpus

We next replicated the profile on a second corpus. The AH2AC2 benchmark (Dizdarević et al., 2025) independently released 18581858 two-player games from the same platform and community; the two collections share no game records. Replayed through the identical pipeline, this corpus has a gap of +27.62​[+27.27,+27.97]​pp+27.62~[+27.27,+27.97]\,\text{pp} against the hanab.live corpus’s +26.16​[+25.31,+26.99]​pp+26.16~[+25.31,+26.99]\,\text{pp}, both clustered by game (AH2AC2 has no player identifiers, so pair clustering is not possible). Its category profile correlates with that of the hanab.live corpus at r=0.97r=0.97, and it shows the same indirect-reference excess. Its differences are consistent with its selection rule, and on the sub-population the two corpora share, the cell values agree closely (+50.4+50.4 against +50.5​pp+50.5\,\text{pp} on color-known cards). The structure and the indirect-reference excess are properties of the community’s play, not of how the hanab.live corpus was built (Appendix E).

3.1.3 Where no level approaches the human gap

On the situations both populations share, humans match level 5 where it plays most often (fresh color-hint plays, +40.9​[+38.2,+43.4]​pp+40.9~[+38.2,+43.4]\,\text{pp} against +40.3​pp+40.3\,\text{pp}) and exceed it modestly elsewhere. One situation is different in kind.

The two populations differ not only in a situation’s gap but in how often they enter it at all (Table 1). The dominant shared situation is a mirror image: level 5 puts 40.4%40.4\% of its plays into the fresh color-hint response, against 29.0%29.0\% for humans. Indirect reference shows the opposite pattern: humans enter it 2.64%2.64\% of the time against level 5’s 0.28%0.28\%, and they play unhinted cards 2.9%2.9\% (newest card) and 2.5%2.5\% (older cards) of the time, where level 5 almost never does. Level 5 does not merely have a smaller gap in these situations; it seldom enters them.

Indirect reference: a taught convention, rare in level 5’s play.

Where the partner’s hint touched a different card, humans reach +61.3​[+54.4,+66.0]​pp+61.3~[+54.4,+66.0]\,\text{pp} against level 5’s +13.7​pp+13.7\,\text{pp} (n=238n=238 human plays); for rank hints the values are +41.1​[+31.9,+48.8]+41.1~[+31.9,+48.8] against +10.3​pp+10.3\,\text{pp}. The sharpest case is an unhinted card played immediately after a color hint that touched another card (n=193n=193). There, the literal failure probability is 69.6%69.6\%, but the actual failure rate is only 5.7%5.7\% (Appendix Table 6). Level 5 rarely makes this play, and its gap there is small (Appendix Fig. 10). The human pattern matches a taught convention (the community’s finesse) in which a hint about one card tells the partner to play a different card from an agreed slot (§4 discusses why the hierarchy may lack it).

Unhinted cards.

Humans reach +48.8​[+38.4,+55.6]​pp+48.8~[+38.4,+55.6]\,\text{pp} on unhinted newest cards and +43.2​[+31.1,+51.5]​pp+43.2~[+31.1,+51.5]\,\text{pp} on older ones, against +23.5+23.5 and +18.3​pp+18.3\,\text{pp} for level 5. Most of these human plays (286286 of 484484) follow a hint to another card, which places them in indirect reference. On the remaining plays, mostly after a partner play or discard, the human gap is +29.4​[+17.3,+40.1]​pp+29.4~[+17.3,+40.1]\,\text{pp} against level 5’s +24.0​pp+24.0\,\text{pp}, a difference of +5.3​[−7.7,+17.1]​pp+5.3~[-7.7,+17.1]\,\text{pp} (Appendix Table 6).

The largest differences survive matching on card configuration.

Indirect reference sits in merged cells of the shared taxonomy, which collect the finer situations that did not reach every population’s nminn_{\min}. A single label can therefore hold different plays for different populations, so we asked whether the split survives a finer classification. Splitting the two indirect-reference cells by the played card’s own hint history shows that it does (Appendix Fig. 10), and the difference has three parts that all point the same way. Occupancy: humans enter “after the partner color-hinted a different card” mostly holding unhinted cards, the finesse configuration, while the hierarchy’s rare entries hold rank-known or fully-identified cards. The human-specific sub-cells are nearly empty for every agent level, and that emptiness is itself a finding. Rate on matched sub-populations: where both populations do occupy a sub-cell, the difference remains. On the finesse sub-cells humans read +63.9+63.9 and +45.4​pp+45.4\,\text{pp} against level 5’s +6.1+6.1 and +1.6​pp+1.6\,\text{pp}; on the color-known sub-cell, +50.5+50.5 against +26.3​pp+26.3\,\text{pp} with non-overlapping intervals; and this color-known sub-cell agrees closely across the two corpora (§3.1.2). Configuration: which cards a population holds when it acts in these situations suggests a different rule for when such a play is allowed. (The merged shared-taxonomy cells of Fig. 1 average over this composition, which is why their values sit below the frozen-cell values quoted here.) Thus the finer classification does not dissolve the finding; it sharpens it.

3.2 Where the conventions are used

To locate the gap, we attach to each play its context (turn, the hint history of the played card, the partner’s immediately preceding action, hand position, and token state) and ask when, in which situations, and in which feature of the game state it sits.

3.2.1 The gap peaks in the mid-game

We first broke the gap down by turn. For levels 2–5 the gap follows an inverted U over the game: close to zero in the opening (+3.5+3.5 to +6.8​pp+6.8\,\text{pp} in turns 0–4), peaking in the mid-game (+36.7​pp+36.7\,\text{pp} at level 5, in the 5-turn bin starting at turn 2020), then falling to between +4.1+4.1 and +6.2​pp+6.2\,\text{pp} late (Fig. 3a). Level 1 stays low throughout (+0.3 to +4.6 pp across all bins). At level 5 the shape comes from the literal risk of the chosen plays: the actual failure rate is flat at 1.9–3.2% across all bins, while the mean literal failure probability rises and falls (Fig. 3b). In this sense conventions are used most in the mid-game: there the plays carry the most literal risk yet fail no more often.

Human play follows the same inverted U (Fig. 3c): similar at the peak (+39.2+39.2 against level 5’s +36.7​pp+36.7\,\text{pp}), but above level 5 in the opening bin (+18.3+18.3 against +6.8​pp+6.8\,\text{pp}) and in every late bin from turn 40 on (6 of 6 bins). The human gap rises earlier and stays high longer than the agents’.

3.2.2 One situation contributes most of level 5’s gap

We next sorted every play into the five hand-crafted situations. One situation dominates: a card played immediately after the partner color-hinted it. A color hint gives the suit and says nothing about the rank, so playing at once is reckless by the literal reading. At level 5 such plays have a mean literal failure probability of 41.1%41.1\% but fail only 0.8%0.8\% of the time, a gap of +40.3​[+39.7,+40.9]​pp+40.3~[+39.7,+40.9]\,\text{pp}. The situation grows from 18.1%18.1\% of plays at level 1 to 40.4%40.4\% at level 5, while its gap grows from +1.0+1.0 to +40.3​pp+40.3\,\text{pp} (Table 1). That one situation contributes 75.1%75.1\% of level 5’s total gap (share ×\times gap in Table 1, over the level-5 total). To a first approximation, the rise of the gap with level reflects both partners’ step-by-step adoption of one rule: a color hint marks a card as playable.

Unhinted plays change sign across the OBL hierarchy. They are rare and, read literally, risky. Level 1 loses more often than literal chance predicts (−13.9​[−17.6,−9.9]​pp-13.9~[-17.6,-9.9]\,\text{pp} on the newest card), while level 5 reaches +23.5​[+17.3,+29.6]​pp+23.5~[+17.3,+29.6]\,\text{pp} in the same situation. One reading is that the absence of a warning carries information: had the newest card been dangerous, the partner might have acted. In human play, most unhinted plays instead follow a hint to another card (§3.1).

3.2.3 At level 5 the gap tracks what the played card is known to be

We then read the induced categories across levels to see which feature of the game state carries the gap (full cross-level reading: Appendix A). At level 5 the induced categories explain R2=0.570R^{2}=0.570 of the per-play residual variance out of sample, against 0.2150.215 for the five hand-crafted situations (Appendix Fig. 6). The carrier moves. At levels 2–3 the main split is hand position; by level 4 it is the played card’s hint history; at level 5 it is color-only knowledge itself, what the card is known to be rather than how fresh the hint was. The two highest-gap categories in the whole taxonomy are delayed color-only plays, played two to three actions after the hint (+62.2​[+60.1,+64.0]​pp+62.2~[+60.1,+64.0]\,\text{pp}) and four or more (+62.2​[+60.0,+64.2]​pp+62.2~[+60.0,+64.2]\,\text{pp}), above the largest fresh-hint categories (Appendix Fig. 5). The hand-crafted map filed these plays under hinted earlier at a diluted +6.4​pp+6.4\,\text{pp}. Thus the hint, or the later absence of a warning, carried information beyond literal content.

3.3 What removing conventions costs

If high-gap channels mark conventions the policy relies on, then blocking them should cost more score than blocking equally frequent plays at random (design in §2.5). It does, but only when several channels are blocked together, and how it does is the finding: the taxonomy ranks categories by their contribution to the gap, and that ranking does not predict what removing a channel costs.

3.3.1 Blocking the color-hint response reroutes the convention rather than destroying it

We first masked the OBL hierarchy’s dominant convention as a whole. Blocking the immediate response to a partner color hint, for both players, changes score by −2.03​[−2.25,−1.81]-2.03~[-2.25,-1.81] points at level 5 (24.10→22.0724.10\rightarrow 22.07). Blocking it for one player has a little under half that effect (−0.92​[−1.10,−0.73]-0.92~[-1.10,-0.73]), and only the blocked player’s gap moves (+22.0​[+21.43,+22.48]→+15.5​[+14.94,+15.97]​pp+22.0~[+21.43,+22.48]\rightarrow+15.5~[+14.94,+15.97]\,\text{pp}, against +20.6​[+20.16,+21.13]→+20.1​[+19.56,+20.56]​pp+20.6~[+20.16,+21.13]\rightarrow+20.1~[+19.56,+20.56]\,\text{pp} for the partner; Appendix D).

But the blocked convention is not destroyed; it is rerouted. Under the immediacy mask the displaced plays reappear one turn later: the hinted earlier share doubles (34%→66%34\%\rightarrow 66\%) and its gap triples (+6.4​[+5.9,+6.9]→+17.5​[+17.1,+18.0]​pp+6.4~[+5.9,+6.9]\rightarrow+17.5~[+17.1,+18.0]\,\text{pp}) at an unchanged loss rate. The convention’s content survives; only its timing breaks, and the score loss is consistent with a cost of delay. Removing these plays instead, by forbidding the play of color-hinted-only cards altogether, changes score by −5.77​[−6.04,−5.49]-5.77~[-6.04,-5.49] points and collapses the gap to +3.5​[+3.17,+3.74]​pp+3.5~[+3.17,+3.74]\,\text{pp}, with the replaced actions shifting toward discards (40%40\%; Appendix D). The two masks leave different marks on the time course (Fig. 4a). The same immediacy mask at level 2 changes score by −1.21​[−1.38,−1.04]-1.21~[-1.38,-1.04]: the cue matters there too, but less.

3.3.2 Single masks cost little beyond generic disruption

We next asked whether the observational ranking predicts the cost of removal. We masked each of the top eight categories by observational contribution (share ×\times gap) one at a time (Fig. 4b). The three low-gap control categories give excess costs of +0.05​[−0.08,+0.18]+0.05~[-0.08,+0.18], +0.09​[+0.01,+0.18]+0.09~[+0.01,+0.18] and −0.00​[−0.10,+0.10]-0.00~[-0.10,+0.10] points, so the control curve is accurate to about a tenth of a point: the size of the single-mask excesses below, and an order of magnitude below the joint-mask interaction of §3.3. Only the two largest-contribution categories have negative excess estimates (−0.12​[−0.25,+0.01]-0.12~[-0.25,+0.01] and −0.09​[−0.23,+0.03]-0.09~[-0.23,+0.03] points), and both intervals reach zero. Apart from category #6, the others lie between −0.02-0.02 and +0.03+0.03. With eight categories, two of which carry most of the leverage, we do not read a dose–response relation into them (Appendix D). Even the top category is mostly generic disruption. Category #1 holds 12.6%12.6\% of plays at +57​pp+57\,\text{pp}, and masking it changes score by −0.39​[−0.51,−0.26]-0.39~[-0.51,-0.26] points raw, but a random mask at the same trigger rate already changes it by −0.27-0.27 (Appendix Table 5); the excess specific to the convention is only −0.12​[−0.25,+0.01]-0.12~[-0.25,+0.01]. Thus most of a single mask’s cost is disruption, not lost meaning.

Masking category #6 raises the score beyond the random mask (excess +0.25​[+0.12,+0.38]+0.25~[+0.12,+0.38] points). A pre-registered out-of-sample replication gives a smaller excess (+0.12​[+0.04,+0.20]+0.12~[+0.04,+0.20] pooled; Appendix D). We read this as no detectable positive value for this convention, with the first estimate inflated by selecting among eight categories.

3.3.3 Joint masks cost far more than the sum of single masks

If single masks are cheap because meaning reroutes, then closing the substitutes together should cost more than their sum. It does. Masking the top eight categories together changes score by −1.84-1.84 points, against −0.77-0.77 for the sum of the eight single masks, a super-additive interaction of −1.08​[−1.47,−0.72]-1.08~[-1.47,-0.72] points (joint minus summed; Fig. 4c), and lowers the total gap by a third, from 21.321.3 to 14.3​[+14.00,+14.68]​pp14.3~[+14.00,+14.68]\,\text{pp} (Appendix Table 5). This is consistent with rerouting: each single mask leaves substitute channels open, and joint masks close them together (the redistribution is in Appendix D).

The interventions push both agents off their training distribution, so these costs are upper bounds under retraining: they price a channel for this fixed pair of policies.

4 Discussion

In this study, we placed human play and the OBL hierarchy on one scale, broke the convention gap down by situation and by turn, and intervened on the agents’ policies against a frequency-matched control. We found that the two populations behave alike in frequent situations, differ in indirect reference, where no level approaches the human gap, and that a convention’s gap contribution does not predict what its removal costs.

Are humans and the OBL hierarchy different?

On the conventions the populations share (everything frequent), they are similar cell by cell, and humans are not significantly closer to level 5 than to level 2. The differences that survive every control are differences in kind, not only in size. Indirect reference shows a human gap that no level approaches: +50.5+50.5 against level 5’s +26.3​pp+26.3\,\text{pp} on the color-known sub-cell, replicated across two independently collected corpora. On unhinted cards that do not follow a hint to another card, the human gap differs from level 5’s by +5.3​[−7.7,+17.1]​pp+5.3~[-7.7,+17.1]\,\text{pp}. Humans also enter indirect reference far more often, and their gap rises earlier and stays high longer. The score-selected AH2AC2 corpus shows the same pattern, and clones trained on human play keep the shared conventions while losing the human-specific cells (Appendix H). The populations have similar gaps on the conventions they share and differ on indirect reference.

Gap contribution is not importance.

The split in §3.3 may apply beyond Hanabi. Removing the eight highest-contribution conventions cuts the total gap by a third but costs under two points of score, consistent with rerouting. The cost appears only when the substitutes are closed together, and then it is more than additive. A channel’s gap contribution and how hard it is to replace are therefore different quantities. Any interpretability method that ranks channels by an observational measure and reads that ranking as importance may inherit this problem; the fix is joint ablation against a matched null (§3.3).

What ZSC gets, and what it does not.

Off-belief learning’s level 1 is trained to read past actions only for their literal content, which needs no shared convention. Human players appear to coordinate the opposite way: they arrive already sharing a taught system (Appendix E.5), and their gap rises earlier in the game than the agents’ (§3.2). Indirect reference suggests what is missing: a representation of hints as speech acts about the whole hand (Frank and Goodman, 2012) rather than as signals about the touched card. Off-belief learning reads each past action as if a fixed base policy had produced it, so a hint on card A carries only what that policy put into it, and level 5 seldom plays card B after it. Depth alone does not account for the difference (Appendix F.7). One interpretation is that a hierarchy whose beliefs rest on a fixed base policy cannot express such a hint.

Supporting analyses.

The appendix adds four results: the realized gap depends on the partner (lower level in seat 0; Appendix B); the agent-grown taxonomy transfers to human play (Appendix E); depth of reasoning does not separate the populations (Appendix F); and clones of both populations reproduce the split between shared conventions and human-specific cells (Appendix H).

What the estimates cover.

The category analysis is descriptive: categories are defined by the action the policy chose, so a category’s gap says how far its plays depart from the literal prediction, not what would happen if the situation were created on purpose. §3.3 supplies the causal complement for the agents’ own conventions; indirect reference cannot be priced this way, because no level enters it often enough to mask. The human corpus comes from a community that publishes and teaches a convention system, so its estimates describe taught play, not typical human play; the pattern replicates on a second, score-selected corpus. All of this is one game; the method needs only an exact literal baseline and a maskable policy.

Reproducibility

The metric implementation is public, released with the previous study (Fukushima et al., 2026), and used at a pinned commit. Every game is replay-verified against its ground-truth score, all numbers were recomputed by a separate audit pipeline, and all our intervals but one bootstrap (Appendix G) reproduce exactly from recorded seeds.
