Appendix A The metric and the category-induction method

This appendix defines the literal observer behind Eq. 1, the context descriptor and cell-size rule used to induce categories, and how the literal posterior rises with level.

A.1 The literal observer and a worked example

At a play action, the literal observer knows, for every card in the acting player’s hand, the set of identities consistent with all positive and negative hint constraints received so far, and it counts copies over every visible zone (the partner’s hand, the discard pile, the fireworks). Because a hint that touches one card constrains the identities available to another, the observer computes the joint distribution over the whole hand, weighting each joint assignment by the number of ways to draw it without replacement from the hidden pool, and marginalizes to the played card. The probability that the played card is unplayable under this distribution is the play’s literal failure probability P⁡(life loss)P(\text{life loss}); Eq. 1 averages it over a set of plays and subtracts the realized failure rate.

A schematic example with five plays illustrates the arithmetic (the values here are illustrative, not data). Suppose the literal failure probabilities of five played cards are 0.400.40, 0.400.40, 0.400.40, 0.200.20 and 0.600.60, and exactly one of the five plays fails. The mean literal failure probability, the literal price of the plays, is 0.400.40; the realized failure rate is 0.200.20; the gap is +20+20 percentage points: the plays succeeded more often than their literal information justified. A gap near zero does not mean the players were well informed, only that their success rate matches the literal price of the plays they chose. The gap is signed: plays can beat or miss their literal price. It cannot exceed the mean literal price.

Two properties matter for everything downstream. First, the baseline is exact: there is no learned component, so a decomposition of the aggregate (by turn, by situation, by category) is free of model error. Second, the observer conditions on observation content but not on action choice: the fact that the partner chose this hint at this moment carries no weight. What the choice itself conveys can show up in the gap, but need not: subsets of plays with gaps of opposite sign can cancel, and plays whose outcome literal information fixes give a gap of exactly zero.

A.2 The six-component descriptor

Every play is described by six components of its context:

  1. 1.

    Partner’s immediately preceding action: play, discard, color hint or rank hint, each hint distinguished by whether it touched the played card (touch) or a different card (other), or no preceding action (first move).

  2. 2.

    Hint relation to the board (hints only): whether the hinted color’s stack is open, or the hinted rank is currently needed on some stack.

  3. 3.

    Hint history of the played card: the ordered pattern of hint types that ever touched it (none, C, R, CR, RC, CC+, RR+, or mixed, meaning three or more).

  4. 4.

    Lag: actions since the last hint that touched the card (11, 22–33, 4+4{+}, or unhinted). In two-player play only odd lags occur, so lag 22–33 means exactly one own action between the hint and the play.

  5. 5.

    Hand position: newest card or older.

  6. 6.

    Hint-token stock: 00, 11–22, or 3+3{+} tokens.

The cross-product yields 303–374 observed context types per level with a heavy-tailed frequency distribution; the number of types needed to cover 90%90\% of plays is, per level, OBL1=90, OBL2=74, OBL3=72, OBL4=70, OBL5=71.

A.3 Cell size, backoff, and the split

The minimum cell size is derived, not chosen. With per-play residual standard deviation ss (empirically 0.18–0.30 across levels, discovery half), estimating a cell mean to ±5​pp\pm 5\,\text{pp} at 95%95\% confidence requires nmin=⌈(1.96​s/0.05)2⌉n_{\min}=\lceil(1.96\,s/0.05)^{2}\rceil, giving 52–139 from level 1 to level 5. A ±3​pp\pm 3\,\text{pp} target would demand cells of 386386 plays at level 5. Types that large cover only 77–82% (OBL2–5; OBL1 53%) of plays, below the 90%90\% coverage we required, so more plays would fall into merged cells.

Types below nminn_{\min} merge by a fixed backoff ladder: drop tokens, then coarsen lag, then drop the board relation, then collapse hint history to its last type, then drop position, leaving at worst the partner’s preceding action alone. No play therefore falls into an opaque other bucket, and every merged cell retains a readable label. Categories and the CART tree are fit on a discovery half (games split 50/50 within level and seed, with a recorded split seed); every reported statistic (cell means, intervals, FDR flags, R2R^{2}) comes from the held-out estimation half (Table 2). The per-category bootstrap intervals reproduce only up to bootstrap error (Appendix G).

A.4 How the literal posterior rises with level

The mean literal posterior is a property of which plays a policy selects, not of the game. In self-play it rises from 7.8%7.8\% (level 1) to 24.1%24.1\% (level 5); the previous study reports this rise and the same plays by hint count [Fukushima et al., 2026]. We split this rise into two simultaneous shifts. Composition: higher levels shift plays from cards touched by two or more hints to cards touched by one. The share of plays on a card touched by exactly one hint grows from 39%39\% to 61%61\%, while plays on cards touched by two or more hints shrink from 56%56\% to 38%38\%. Within-stratum: even among one-hint plays, higher levels accept literally riskier ones. The mean posterior within that stratum climbs from 12.8%12.8\% to 37.3%37.3\% while the realized loss rate of the same plays falls from 7.8%7.8\% to 2.9%2.9\%. A Kitagawa split of the rise [Kitagawa, 1955] puts +1.0​pp+1.0\,\text{pp} in composition and +15.2​pp+15.2\,\text{pp} within strata, with the composition term evaluated at level-1 stratum posteriors and the within-stratum term at level-5 shares. This is an accounting identity and assigns no cause. At these weights the composition term is small, because the shrinking share of plays on cards no hint touched partially offsets the growing one-hint share.

A.5 The induced taxonomy: full construction and cross-level results

A.5.1 Data-induced categories

The five situations of §2.4 (fresh color hint, fresh rank hint, hinted earlier, unhinted newest, unhinted older; the hand-crafted map below) explain only 0.2150.215 of per-play residual variance at level 5. We therefore induce categories from the data, using the descriptor of §A.2 and the cell-size, backoff and split rules of §A.3; all reported statistics come from the estimation half with game-clustered bootstrap intervals and Benjamini–Hochberg control at q=0.05q=0.05 [Benjamini and Hochberg, 1995].

The induced taxonomy yields 105105 categories at level 5 and explains R2=0.570R^{2}=0.570 out of sample, matched by a depth-4 CART tree [Breiman et al., 1984] at 0.5710.571, against 0.2150.215 for the hand-crafted map (Fig. 6). At level 1 the taxonomy explains R2=0.058R^{2}=0.058 and the CART tree 0.0690.069. The low values do not mean that level 1 lacks structure. Its tree splits first on whether any hint touched the played card (Table 3), and its plays on cards no hint touched have negative gaps, −13.9​pp-13.9\,\text{pp} on the newest card and −9.8​pp-9.8\,\text{pp} on older cards (Table 1). These plays are rare (2.0%2.0\% and 2.3%2.3\% of level 1’s plays), so they can explain little per-play variance.

A.5.2 The knowledge state, not the freshness of the hint, carries the gap

Reading the trees across levels shows the phenomenon relocating (Table 3). At levels 2–3 the root split is hand position; by level 4 it is the played card’s hint history; at level 5 it is color-only knowledge outright. As the OBL hierarchy deepens, what the card is known to be rises from a sub-split to the primary axis of the policy’s gap. What carries the gap is not the freshness of the cue but the knowledge state the cue produced.

The sharpest evidence comes from lag, the number of actions since the last hint that touched the card. If hint meaning decayed over time, gaps would fall with lag. Instead, the two highest-gap categories in the whole level-5 taxonomy are delayed color-only plays: the card was color-hinted, the player did something else first, then played it. The lag-22–33 category reads +62.2​[+60.1,+64.0]​pp+62.2~[+60.1,+64.0]\,\text{pp} and the lag-4+4{+} category +62.2​[+60.0,+64.2]​pp+62.2~[+60.0,+64.2]\,\text{pp}, above the two largest fresh-hint categories at +56.8​[+56.4,+57.2]+56.8~[+56.4,+57.2] and +55.6​[+55.1,+56.2]​pp+55.6~[+55.1,+56.2]\,\text{pp} (all four values are level-5 self-play, estimation half). Thus the hint, or the later absence of a warning, carried information beyond literal content; the gap does not say which. The hand-crafted map filed all of these under hinted earlier at a diluted +6.4​pp+6.4\,\text{pp}, which is how a +62.2​pp+62.2\,\text{pp} category disappears into a +6.4​pp+6.4\,\text{pp} situation.

Two further structures the hand-crafted map misses. Hand position separates otherwise matched fresh-color categories by 12.7–32.5 pp (levels 2–5), and token scarcity shifts the same situation by a few points (+54.4 at 0 tokens vs +55.5/+57.0 at 1–2/3+ tokens). Despite roughly a hundred categories per level, a handful of categories carry 80%80\% of each level’s total gap (per level: OBL1=5, OBL2=7, OBL3=7, OBL4=7, OBL5=8). Seed-to-seed differences sit in the tail of the taxonomy (Appendix C).

This analysis is descriptive: categories condition on the action the policy chose, so a category’s gap says how far its plays depart from the literal prediction, not what would happen if the situation were induced. §3.3 supplies the causal complement.

Appendix B Mixed-level play

This appendix gives the analysis behind the statement in §4 that the realized gap depends on the partner. §B.1 reports all ten mixed-level pairings, §B.2 localizes the effect in the fresh color-hint cue, and Appendix C repeats the per-agent comparison of §B.1 across seed combinations.

B.1 Per-agent gaps in mixed-level play

The self-play ladder rises with level. It does not say what happens when two levels meet. We played all ten mixed-level pairings (10001000 games each, replay-verified) and computed Δ\Delta separately for each side’s own plays (Fig. 7). In every game of this design the lower level held seat 0 and moved first, and this analysis uses no seat-reversed games. Each side’s statistics, and their comparison with self-play (which pools both seats), therefore include any seat effect. For scale, in the level-5 self-play baseline of §3.3, seat 0 has a gap of +22.0​[+21.43,+22.48]​pp+22.0~[+21.43,+22.48]\,\text{pp} and seat 1 +20.6​[+20.16,+21.13]​pp+20.6~[+20.16,+21.13]\,\text{pp}. The previous study reports level 1’s own gaps in these games [Fukushima et al., 2026]; the analysis below (the per-agent split across all ten pairings, its localization, and its seed behavior) is new here.

The gap an agent realizes depends on its partner.

Paired with a higher level, level 1’s own aggregate gap falls toward zero: from +1.0​[+0.7,+1.3]​pp+1.0~[+0.7,+1.3]\,\text{pp} against level 2 to +0.1​[−0.2,+0.5]​pp+0.1~[-0.2,+0.5]\,\text{pp} against level 5, an interval that includes zero. A near-zero aggregate can still contain plays that depart from the literal prediction: on cards level 1 plays immediately after level 5 color-hinted them, its gap is +1.9​[+1.3,+2.4]​pp+1.9~[+1.3,+2.4]\,\text{pp} (§B.2). The higher-level agent, whose policy is unchanged, has gaps of +8.4​[+8.0,+8.9]+8.4~[+8.0,+8.9] to +9.0​[+8.6,+9.4]​pp+9.0~[+8.6,+9.4]\,\text{pp} across the four level-1 pairings, against its own self-play values of +12.40​[+12.10,+12.71]+12.40~[+12.10,+12.71] to +21.68​[+21.34,+22.02]​pp+21.68~[+21.34,+22.02]\,\text{pp}. One reading of the higher agent’s positive gap is that level 1’s hints tend to mark playable cards, so its hint choices carry some information beyond their literal content. The partner dependence is not confined to one phase of the game: level 5’s entire time course flattens with level distance, its mid-game peak falling from +36.7​pp+36.7\,\text{pp} in self-play to +30.7+30.7 with level 3 and +13.8​pp+13.8\,\text{pp} with level 1 (§B.2, Fig. 8).

The higher agent’s loss rate rises, and score falls.

The higher-level agent appears to keep taking convention-style plays that a level-1 partner’s hints do not license, and its added failures are localized. On plays made immediately after a partner color hint, the situation §3.2 identifies as the OBL hierarchy’s dominant cue, the higher agent’s failure rate rises from 0.8 to 1.0% in self-play to 4.6%4.6\% (level 2) through 13.3%13.3\% (level 5) when the hint comes from level 1. Level 1’s own failure rate in the same situation is 0.7 to 1.4%. Score falls monotonically with level distance, from 21.3721.37 for 1×21\times 2 to 19.3319.33 for 1×51\times 5 (Fig. 7b). From 1×31\times 3 on, the pair scores below level 1’s own self-play value of 21.0921.09: level 1 scores more with a copy of itself than with level 3, 4 or 5.

Levels 2–5 are mutually compatible and blend.

In this seating, the two sides’ gaps lie close together in every pairing among levels 2–5, although the two levels differ in self-play. For 2×52\times 5, for instance, the sides have gaps of +13.4​[+13.0,+13.9]+13.4~[+13.0,+13.9] and +14.0​[+13.6,+14.5]​pp+14.0~[+13.6,+14.5]\,\text{pp}, against self-play values of +12.40+12.40 and +21.68​pp+21.68\,\text{pp}. The common value sits between them, nearer the lower level, and score lands near the lower level’s self-play score. This is consistent with each agent taking mainly the plays its partner’s hints license. It is also what one expects if level kk’s conventions are approximately a subset of level k+1k+1’s, rather than each level developing a separate system of its own.

Both patterns recur across seed combinations.

The level-1 split appears in all 2525 seed combinations of 1×51\times 5, and among levels 2–5 the mean side difference over seed combinations stays within ±0.70​pp\pm 0.70\,\text{pp} (Appendix C).

B.2 The mixed-level cue map

The per-agent time courses under different partners appear in Fig. 8; the cue-level view localizes them. On plays made immediately after a partner color hint, the agent facing a level-1 partner keeps entering the situation (2121 to 27%27\% of its plays) while its loss rate there rises with its own level, from 4.6%4.6\% (level 2) to 13.3%13.3\% (level 5), against 0.8 to 1.0% in self-play, and its cue gap falls to +14.1​pp+14.1\,\text{pp} from a self-play value near +40.3​pp+40.3\,\text{pp}. Level 1 fails rarely in the same situation (loss 0.7 to 1.4%; gap +1.3+1.3 to +2.0​pp+2.0\,\text{pp}). Between levels 2–5 the cue blends unevenly: the lower partner’s cue gap rises above its own self-play value (level 2 with level 5: +30.6​pp+30.6\,\text{pp}) at a loss rate that stays low (0.6%0.6\%), while the higher partner’s falls toward the lower partner’s value (+23.1​pp+23.1\,\text{pp}). Both sides’ overall gaps meet near the blended values of §B.1.

Appendix C Seed robustness

C.1 The seed sweep

Appendix B reports single-seed pairings: one released model per level. This appendix asks whether its two results, the level-1 split and the blend among levels 2–5, depend on which seed models were paired. To test this, every pairing among levels 2–5, plus the level-1×51{\times}5 control, was played for all 2525 seed combinations (seeds a–e on each side, 200200 games per combination; 3500035000 games in total, each replay-verified). The unit of analysis is the seed combination: the primary statistic per level pair is the across-combination mean of the side difference δ=Δhigher−Δlower\delta=\Delta_{\text{higher}}-\Delta_{\text{lower}}, with a tt-based 95%95\% interval over the 2525 combinations (Table 4). The combinations share seed models on each side and are not independent replications, so the tt interval may be too narrow for inference beyond these models. As in Appendix B, the lower level held seat 0 in every game.

Both patterns recur across seed combinations. Among levels 2–5 the mean δ\delta stays within ±0.70​pp\pm 0.70\,\text{pp} of zero for every pairing, an order of magnitude below the control’s +7.77​[+7.33,+8.20]​pp+7.77~[+7.33,+8.20]\,\text{pp}, which is positive in all 2525 combinations (per-combination range +6.3+6.3 to +10.3​pp+10.3\,\text{pp}). The sweep also points to two asymmetries that the single-seed analysis did not show: δ\delta is positive, with an interval above zero, for 2×42{\times}4 (+0.70​[+0.26,+1.14]​pp+0.70~[+0.26,+1.14]\,\text{pp}) and for 2×52{\times}5 (+0.64​[+0.22,+1.07]​pp+0.64~[+0.22,+1.07]\,\text{pp}), so when level 2 is the lower partner the higher side’s gap may be slightly larger. With seats fixed, these differences cannot be separated from seat: in level-5 self-play the two seats’ gaps are +22.0​[+21.43,+22.48]+22.0~[+21.43,+22.48] and +20.6​[+20.16,+21.13]​pp+20.6~[+20.16,+21.13]\,\text{pp} (Appendix B). The 4×54{\times}5 interval touches zero from below (−0.45​[−0.90,−0.00]​pp-0.45~[-0.90,-0.00]\,\text{pp}); given the shared models and the number of intervals, we do not read it as an asymmetry. The last column estimates the share of across-combination variance in δ\delta not explained by game-sampling noise; it rests on bootstrap standard errors and is approximate.

C.2 Self-play across seeds

Self-play gaps vary across the five seed models with standard deviations of 0.61​pp0.61\,\text{pp} (level 2), 0.670.67 (level 3), 1.271.27 (level 4) and 1.53​pp1.53\,\text{pp} (level 5). The spread is larger at higher levels. Per-level ranges overlap across seeds, but the means over seeds rise from +12.34+12.34 (level 2) to +21.11​pp+21.11\,\text{pp} (level 5), and the ordering Δ2<Δ3<Δ4<Δ5\Delta_{2}<\Delta_{3}<\Delta_{4}<\Delta_{5} holds within each of the 5 seeds when models are matched by seed letter.

C.3 Seed heterogeneity sits in the taxonomy tail

Within the induced taxonomy of §2.4, per-seed cell values were checked for the top-ten categories by absolute gap at each of levels 2–5 (4040 cells; 1818 flagged with across-seed excess variance beyond game-sampling noise). Head cells are seed-stable in relative terms: their excess standard deviations are 1.5–2.9 pp (3–9% of gap). Every large-excess flag sits in a tail cell holding at most 0.87% of plays: the widest are a discard-context color cell at level 3 (+13.9 to +44.8, excess 10.8 pp), an unhinted cell at level 4 (+18.1 to +47.8, excess 8.2 pp), and a repeat-color-hint cell at level 5 (+31.5 to +52.4, excess 7.5 pp); each parenthesis gives the range across seeds and the excess standard deviation. Different training runs agree on the head of the taxonomy and differ in its tail.

Appendix D Intervention details

This appendix gives the details behind the intervention results of §3.3: the verification gates, the full condition table, the replication of the one anomalous mask, and a category-level check of the rerouting. Apart from the level-2 contrast, the masks act on the seed-a model of level 5, which is in the released archive but not among the results published with OBL [Hu et al., 2021] (§2.2); the replication adds level-5 seed b and level-4 seed a. The level-5 baseline uses this model on its own environment seeds, and its gap (21.3​pp21.3\,\text{pp}) differs from the ladder value (+21.68​pp+21.68\,\text{pp}).

D.1 Verification gates

Two gates precede every full run. First, the category that the masking code assigns to each play during the game must match the category that the analysis assigns afterwards; on the baseline games the two agree on every play a mask would block (24838/2483824838/24838). Second, the masking code with no mask active must reproduce the baseline games: 1000/10001000/1000 games match action for action, deck and score. All mask conditions share environment seeds with the baseline, and the full 5050-card decks are identical per seed across every condition (1000/1000 for every condition), so score differences are paired per deck. Every condition replays to its ground-truth score.

D.2 The condition table

Targets are the top eight categories by observational contribution (share ×\times gap, estimation half) among categories holding at least 1%1\% of plays, three low-gap controls (two fully identified cells, whose gap is zero by construction, and the large low-gap rank cell at lag 4+4{+}), and cumulative masks of the top 1/2/4/6/81/2/4/6/8 (top-1 coincides with single #1). Frequency-matched random controls suppress the greedy play with probability matched to the trigger rates of targets #1, #4 and #8 (3.76/0.61/0.243.76/0.61/0.24 triggers per game) and define the null cost curve: piecewise linear through the origin and the three controls in realized trigger rate, linearly extrapolated beyond the largest control rate, and re-fit inside every bootstrap draw so the excess interval carries the control curve’s own uncertainty. Rows whose realized trigger rate exceeds the largest control rate (the cumulative top-2, top-4, top-6 and top-8 masks) rely on that extrapolation and are marked † in Table 5; the super-additivity claim in §3.3 uses raw paired costs and does not depend on it.

The three low-gap controls (Table 5) show that the control curve is accurate to about a tenth of a point (§3.3).

Why no dose–response fit is reported.

An ordinary least-squares fit of the eight single-mask excess costs on contribution gives a slope of −2.87​[−4.78,−0.98]-2.87~[-4.78,-0.98] points per unit of contribution (contribution as a probability; interval from the game-level bootstrap) with R2=0.44R^{2}=0.44; on the category’s gap alone R2=0.72R^{2}=0.72, on its share alone 0.110.11. We do not interpret these fits. They rest on eight cells, six of which sit within about one percentage point of contribution of each other, so categories #1 and #2 carry most of the leverage, and neither of their excess intervals excludes zero. The fit is also sensitive to category #6, whose replication was inconclusive (§D.4). The bootstrap interval treats the eight categories as fixed and therefore says nothing about how excess cost would vary across other categories.

D.3 Redistribution under the masks

Masking a color cell delays some of its plays. Under the top-1 mask the delayed color-only category (lag 22–33) grows from 1.5%1.5\% of plays to 5.9%5.9\% at a gap of +54.2​pp+54.2\,\text{pp}; under the top-8 mask it reaches 16.3%16.3\% at +52.9​pp+52.9\,\text{pp}. The total gap falls from 21.321.3 to 14.3​[+14.00,+14.68]​pp14.3~[+14.00,+14.68]\,\text{pp} while score falls −1.84-1.84 points. The single-mask and cumulative results are plotted in Fig. 4b and c.

D.4 Replication of the category-6 anomaly

The apparent score improvement from masking category #6 was re-tested out of sample before being interpreted: fresh decks disjoint from every prior condition, three agents (level-5 seeds a and b, level-4 seed a), each with its own baseline and frequency-matched random control, and a decision rule fixed in advance (replicates if all three excesses are positive and at least two per-agent intervals exclude zero; fails if the pooled interval contains zero). Outcome: inconclusive. The excesses are positive for all three agents (+0.14​[−0.003,+0.292]+0.14~[-0.003,+0.292], +0.15​[+0.035,+0.274]+0.15~[+0.035,+0.274], +0.06​[−0.098,+0.205]+0.06~[-0.098,+0.205]) and the inverse-variance pooled excess is +0.12​[+0.04,+0.20]+0.12~[+0.04,+0.20], but only 11 per-agent interval excludes zero, and the raw score gain in Table 5 (+0.10+0.10 points) did not reproduce. The supported reading is that this convention carries no detectable positive value (“cheaper than random disruption,” not beneficial), and that the first estimate was inflated by selecting among eight categories. The substitution pattern does reproduce: under the mask, 48–62% of masked plays substitute into another rank hint, as in the original run.

D.5 Taxonomy validation on the intervention games

Applying the frozen taxonomy to the masked games checks the rerouting at category level, independently of the score analysis. Under the immediacy mask, level-5’s color-only lag-1 categories empty by construction (29.6% of baseline plays at +55​pp+55\,\text{pp}) and many displaced plays reappear as color-only lag-22–33 plays at nearly undiminished gap: that category’s share rises from 1.5% to 16.7% at +53​pp+53\,\text{pp}, with a smaller spill into lag 4+4{+} (3.1% →\rightarrow 6.1% at +32​pp+32\,\text{pp}). Under the persistent mask the color-only categories stay empty (0.0%) and play shifts onto fully identified cards, whose gap is zero by construction (35.6% →\rightarrow 60.0% of plays). Level 2 reroutes less. Its delayed color-only gap at baseline is +17​pp+17\,\text{pp}, against level-5’s +41​pp+41\,\text{pp}, and under the immediacy mask its color-only lag-22–33 share reaches 2.5%, against level-5’s 16.7%.

Appendix E Human corpus

This appendix documents the two human corpora (provenance, filters, clustering and the convention community they come from) and gives the full versions of the human results summarized in §3.1.

E.1 Provenance and filters

The corpus is drawn from public logs of two-player, no-variant games on the hanab.live platform [Hanab Live, 2026], the platform the convention community plays on, with usernames replaced by salted hashes before any analysis. Two filters define the analysis set. The completed-games filter removes games whose logs end abnormally (timeouts, terminations, or logs that stop with cards in the deck and no terminal state). The bot exclusion has two tiers: a game-level tier for verified bot families matched by account-name pattern, and an account-level tier removing plays by flagged accounts (accounts that play almost only with verified bots, pairs of accounts with identical timing statistics, and accounts whose game notes carry a bot’s version tag; criteria as in the previous study [Fukushima et al., 2026], identified by hashed id). The result is 425425 games, 90179017 plays, 155155 players and 9595 pairs. A sensitivity corpus applying only the verified-bot tier holds 598598 games / 1308913089 plays and gives +27.52​[+25.21,+29.69]​pp+27.52~[+25.21,+29.69]\,\text{pp}.

E.2 Statements shared with the prior paper

This corpus, its filters and its posteriors are those of the previous study that introduced the convention gap [Fukushima et al., 2026] (“the prior paper” below).

Posterior variant. Both papers report the joint (full-hand) posterior, which gives a corpus headline of +26.16​pp+26.16\,\text{pp}. The per-card approximation gives +28.20​pp+28.20\,\text{pp} on the same corpus. The two variants are never mixed within a figure or a comparison.

The Tier-1 filter, as implemented. The Tier-1 filter removes every game in which a verified bot account made a play. One game in which a verified bot only hinted and discarded is therefore retained; excluding it as well gives 424424 games and 9,0119{,}011 plays and a gap of +26.18​pp+26.18\,\text{pp}, against +26.16​pp+26.16\,\text{pp} [Fukushima et al., 2026].

E.3 Corpus identity with the prior paper

The identity is exact, not approximate, and was established by a three-part check: (i) the game sets are identical (sorted id lists, symmetric difference empty); (ii) the filter chain is the same code, imported rather than reimplemented; and (iii) the joint posteriors agree play-for-play, bit-identically, over all 90179017 plays against an independent run of the prior paper’s engine on the raw logs.

E.4 Clustering: pair against game

Pairs recur across games, so the primary human intervals cluster at the pair level (9595 pairs); game-clustered intervals are narrower. Side by side, joint posterior: corpus gap +26.16​[+24.05,+28.28]+26.16~[+24.05,+28.28] (pair) against [+25.32,+27.01][+25.32,+27.01] (game); Tier-1-only sensitivity +27.52​[+25.21,+29.69]+27.52~[+25.21,+29.69] (pair) against [+26.79,+28.26][+26.79,+28.26] (game). The documented exceptions are the nearest-level bootstrap and the mixture fit of Appendix F (§F.2 and §F.3), which are game-clustered by design, for comparability with the agent corpora; their pair-clustered sensitivity is in §F.4.

E.5 The convention community

The platform’s community publishes and teaches a convention system [H-Group, 2026]: play hints and the focus rule, chop and save conventions, and the finesse family are written down rather than negotiated at the table. The human corpus therefore describes taught play, not typical human play. Pair experience, counted within the corpus, moves the gap little: stratifying pairs by games played together gives +23.6​[+20.2,+26.8]​pp+23.6~[+20.2,+26.8]\,\text{pp} (one game together, 3636 pairs), +25.7​[+23.5,+27.8]​pp+25.7~[+23.5,+27.8]\,\text{pp} (2–4 games), and +26.6​[+23.8,+29.7]​pp+26.6~[+23.8,+29.7]\,\text{pp} (five or more), and near-strangers (one game together, both players in at most two corpus games) reach +22.1​[+17.8,+26.0]​pp+22.1~[+17.8,+26.0]\,\text{pp}. This is consistent with players who arrive already sharing a taught system.

E.6 The AH2AC2 corpus

The replication corpus (§3.1.2) is processed identically from the open release: conversion to the common game format, replay verification against the released scores (18581858 of 18581858 games reproduce exactly), then the same completed-games criterion, which removes 106106 games. Every one is a verifiable “no further points possible” early ending, a completed game our criterion nonetheless excludes; they are retained as a sensitivity (+27.59​[+27.26,+27.92]​pp+27.59~[+27.26,+27.92]\,\text{pp} on the full release against +27.62​[+27.27,+27.97]​pp+27.62~[+27.27,+27.97]\,\text{pp} on the filtered corpus). The open data carry no player identifiers, so the bot exclusion cannot be applied and all AH2AC2 intervals cluster by game. Score selection in that collection (minimum recorded score 1313; no strikeouts) is consistent with its higher aggregate (§3.1.2); restricting the hanab.live corpus to games at or above the same floor gives +27.20​[+26.29,+28.04]​pp+27.20~[+26.29,+28.04]\,\text{pp} over 338338 games.

E.7 The shared taxonomy ranked by the human–level-5 difference

Ranking the cells of the shared taxonomy (§2.4) by the absolute difference between the human and level-5 gaps (Fig. 9) ignores how often each cell occurs. The split in §3.1 is an accounting identity and assigns no cause. Its within-cell term weights each cell’s gap difference by the human share of plays. Its other term weights each cell’s share difference by the level-5 gap. The three largest differences are the two indirect-reference cells and a delayed color cell. Level 5’s gap is higher on three newest-card cells played right after a hint and, by small amounts, on three merged cells; the cells that are zero by construction close the list at exactly zero. The two indirect-reference cells are merged residual cells, which the next subsection resolves.

E.8 The indirect-reference category, decomposed

Table 1’s indirect-reference rows are merged cells, defined only by the partner’s preceding action, and their contents differ across populations (Fig. 10). The numbers in this paragraph use the frozen level-5 taxonomy on the full corpus, the basis of the right-hand panels of Fig. 10; on that basis the human color cell holds 238238 plays. Decomposed by the played card’s own hint history, it is 81.1%81.1\% unhinted cards (the finesse configuration, +63.9​pp+63.9\,\text{pp} over 193193 plays), 18.1%18.1\% color-known cards (+50.5​pp+50.5\,\text{pp}), and a remainder too small to estimate. The left-hand panels of Fig. 10 use a different basis, the shared taxonomy on estimation halves, whose residual cell is broader because it must be supported by all six populations; its unhinted share is therefore lower than the frozen-cell figure quoted here, and the two panels are not meant to match. Table 6 gives the reverse decomposition: all unhinted plays split by the partner’s preceding action. In human play, 286286 of the 484484 unhinted plays follow a hint to another card (gap +57.9​[+50.6,+62.7]​pp+57.9~[+50.6,+62.7]\,\text{pp}), against 5555 of 394394 for level 5. On the remaining unhinted plays, humans and level 5 differ by +5.3​[−7.7,+17.1]​pp+5.3~[-7.7,+17.1]\,\text{pp}; in AH2AC2, which keeps no struck-out games, the difference is +9.5​[+2.0,+16.8]​pp+9.5~[+2.0,+16.8]\,\text{pp}. The color-known sub-cell is the composition-matched comparison used in §3.1.2: +50.4​[+47.1,+53.6]​pp+50.4~[+47.1,+53.6]\,\text{pp} in AH2AC2 against +50.5​pp+50.5\,\text{pp} here.

E.9 Replication on the AH2AC2 corpus in full

The corpus above reflects one set of collection and filtering choices. The AH2AC2 benchmark [Dizdarević et al., 2025] independently released 18581858 two-player games collected from the same platform and convention community. The two collections share no game records: content identity over deck and full action sequence matches 00 of 18581858 against the raw hanab.live logs used here. This is therefore an independent collection from the same population (deck-level coincidences exist, but only because the platform deals seeded decks to many tables). Player overlap is unknowable, because the open data carry no player identifiers (§E.6).

Replaying all games through the identical pipeline (replay-verified against the released scores, 1858/18581858/1858; 17521752 games after the completed-games criterion), the corpus realizes +27.62​[+27.27,+27.97]​pp+27.62~[+27.27,+27.97]\,\text{pp} against the hanab.live corpus’s +26.16​[+25.31,+26.99]​pp+26.16~[+25.31,+26.99]\,\text{pp} under the same game-level clustering: above every level of the OBL hierarchy, and +1.46​pp+1.46\,\text{pp} from the hanab.live corpus. The category structure replicates more closely than the aggregate: the frozen-category profile correlates with the hanab.live corpus at r=0.97r=0.97 (excluding the construction-zero cells), the frozen tree transfers at R2=0.338R^{2}=0.338 (hanab.live 0.280.28), and indirect reference has gaps above every agent value (+48.9​[+45.4,+52.1]+48.9~[+45.4,+52.1] for color, +39.9​[+36.2,+43.5]​pp+39.9~[+36.2,+43.5]\,\text{pp} for rank), as do plays of unhinted newest cards (+37.2​[+31.9,+42.2]​pp+37.2~[+31.9,+42.2]\,\text{pp}; Table 6).

The differences are consistent with AH2AC2’s selection rule (minimum score 1313, no strikeouts; mean score 23.4523.45 against 18.5218.52 for the hanab.live corpus). Excluding struck-out games removes games with three failed plays, which raises the aggregate gap mechanically. The rule also nearly eliminates unhinted plays (share 1.7%1.7\% against 5.4%5.4\%) and tilts the indirect-reference cell toward color-known cards. On the sub-population the two corpora share, the cell replicates closely (+50.4+50.4 against +50.5​pp+50.5\,\text{pp} on color-known cards). The category structure and the indirect-reference excess are therefore properties of the community’s play, not of how the hanab.live corpus was constructed. Population-level independence is a different question and stays open (§4).

E.10 The aggregate view on the OBL ladder

The pair-clustered human corpus gap (+26.16​[+24.05,+28.28]​pp+26.16~[+24.05,+28.28]\,\text{pp}) lies above every level of the OBL ladder reported in the prior paper [Fukushima et al., 2026], which runs from +1.57​pp+1.57\,\text{pp} at level 1 to +21.68​pp+21.68\,\text{pp} at level 5 (Table 5 there). This is the aggregate picture behind the top row of Fig. 1. These are differences of aggregate gaps. They are not the per-cell distances of Fig. 2, which average the absolute human–level difference over the shared cells and can order the levels differently.

E.11 The agent-grown taxonomy transfers to people

We freeze §2.4’s level-5 machinery (discovery-half category definitions, category means and the fitted tree, verbatim) and apply it to human plays. The frozen tree explains R2=0.28R^{2}=0.28 of human per-play residual variance out of sample (0.370.37 using the frozen partition with human cell means), against 0.390.39 for a tree grown on human data itself and 0.120.12 for the hand-crafted map. Across the 2626 frozen categories with at least 100100 human plays, human and agent gaps correlate at r=0.70r=0.70 once the 66 categories that are zero for both sides by construction are excluded (r=0.81r=0.81 with them), with human points on or above the diagonal (Fig. 11b).

This transfer is consistent with the metric tracking play rather than how agent games are generated. It is not independent validation: a category’s gap cannot exceed its mean literal failure probability, and the same hint context can carry similar literal risk in both populations, so part of the correlation may reflect these bounds.

Pair experience and zero-shot coordination.

The gap moves little with how often a pair has played together within the corpus (§E.5): near-strangers reach +22.1​[+17.8,+26.0]​pp+22.1~[+17.8,+26.0]\,\text{pp}, against +1.22​[+0.98,+1.45]​pp+1.22~[+0.98,+1.45]\,\text{pp} for level-1 cross-play, pooled over all pairings among five independently trained level-1 models [Fukushima et al., 2026]. Both are zero-shot coordination, of opposite kinds. Level 1 is trained to read past actions only for their literal content, and its gap is similar in self-play and in cross-play. Human players appear to arrive already sharing a taught system. In point estimate, the self-play gaps of the OBL levels lie between the level-1 cross-play and near-stranger values, and level 5’s gap (+21.68​pp+21.68\,\text{pp}) lies inside the near-stranger interval.

Appendix F Depth of reasoning

On the 44 categories where the human value lies within the levels’ range, the agent profile saturates by level 2–3 and humans land at that plateau. Where humans diverge they exceed every level, the opposite pattern from limited recursion. A pre-registered cognitive-hierarchy fit leaves depth unidentified (τ\tau ran to the grid edge in both models) and instead recovers a flat uplift of +14.3​[+13.2,+15.4]​pp+14.3~[+13.2,+15.4]\,\text{pp} on the categories where humans exceed every level (§F.3).

F.1 Distance to the human profile per level

On the shared taxonomy of §2.4 (estimation halves, the basis of Fig. 1), we compute for each level kk the mean per-cell absolute difference to the human profile, Dk=meanc⁡|h⁡(c)−gk​(c)|D_{k}=\operatorname{mean}_{c}\,|h(c)-g_{k}(c)|, with 95% intervals from a joint bootstrap (10,00010{,}000 draws; humans resampled by pair, each agent corpus by game, all six corpora independently per draw; contrasts formed within draws; recorded seed). Over all 2121 shared cells, D1D_{1} through D5D_{5} read 19.0​[+16.9,+20.8]19.0~[+16.9,+20.8], 10.2​[+8.4,+11.9]10.2~[+8.4,+11.9], 8.3​[+6.6,+10.0]8.3~[+6.6,+10.0], 7.1​[+6.1,+8.9]7.1~[+6.1,+8.9] and 7.0​[+5.9,+8.7]​pp7.0~[+5.9,+8.7]\,\text{pp}. Excluding the 1111 cells where the human value exceeds every level’s with bootstrap probability at least 0.870.87 (the rule of §F.2, applied to the shared cells), the remaining core cells read 15.9​[+13.9,+18.0]15.9~[+13.9,+18.0], 4.1​[+2.6,+5.9]4.1~[+2.6,+5.9], 2.7​[+1.5,+4.5]2.7~[+1.5,+4.5], 1.3​[+1.3,+3.5]1.3~[+1.3,+3.5] and 1.7​[+1.5,+3.7]​pp1.7~[+1.5,+3.7]\,\text{pp}. The contrasts localize the approach to the human profile in the first step: on the core cells D1−D2=+11.9​[+10.4,+13.0]​ppD_{1}-D_{2}=+11.9~[+10.4,+13.0]\,\text{pp} against D2−D5=+2.4​[−0.6,+3.5]​ppD_{2}-D_{5}=+2.4~[-0.6,+3.5]\,\text{pp}, an interval that includes zero; over all cells D2−D5=+3.2​[+1.7,+3.7]​ppD_{2}-D_{5}=+3.2~[+1.7,+3.7]\,\text{pp}, so the residual decline past level 2 is carried by the excluded cells. A signed, human-share-weighted sensitivity gives the same shape.

F.2 The nearest-level bootstrap

For each of the 2020 non-zero frozen categories (human n≥100n\geq 100; 66 construction-zero cells dropped), the level profile g1​(c),…,g5​(c)g_{1}(c),\ldots,g_{5}(c) uses each level’s taxonomy corpus (one seed model at level 1, five pooled at levels 2–5) and the human value comes from the full corpus. The nearest-level statistic arg⁡mink​|gk​(c)−h⁡(c)|\arg\min_{k}|g_{k}(c)-h(c)|, recorded as “>5{>}5” when the human value exceeds every level’s, is bootstrapped with 20002000 draws, resampling games in all six corpora independently per draw. Human resampling here is game-clustered by design, for comparability with the agent corpora (a pair-clustered sensitivity is in §F.4). 1616 of the 2020 categories exceed every level with bootstrap probability at least 0.870.87; we call them the above-every-level categories, and they define the indicator of the mixture fit.

F.3 The pre-registered mixture fit

This fit asks a simple question: can the human category profile be written as a mixture of the five level profiles, with the mixing weights set by a single depth parameter τ\tau (how many steps of reasoning a typical human uses)? If depth were what separates humans from the OBL hierarchy, the fit would return a well-identified τ\tau and no residual. The outcome is that τ\tau is not identified (it runs to the edge of its grid) and that a flat uplift on the above-every-level categories fits the data instead.

The specification was fixed before the fit:

  • •

    M1 regresses the human category gaps on a truncated-Poisson(τ)(\tau) mixture of the five level profiles (pmf renormalized on k∈{1,…,5}k\in\{1,\dots,5\}).

  • •

    M2 adds a flat uplift β\beta on the above-every-level categories.

  • •

    Weights are inverse bootstrap variances of the human gaps.

  • •

    Fitting: τ\tau by grid search over [0.05,8][0.05,8] at step 0.010.01, with β\beta in closed form given τ\tau.

  • •

    Uncertainty: a joint bootstrap (20002000 draws, recorded seeds) resampling all six corpora and refitting both models per draw.

  • •

    Pre-registered truncation flags: τ^\hat{\tau} at the grid edge, and Poisson weight on level 5 above 0.40.4 at τ^\hat{\tau}.

Both flags were raised. τ^\hat{\tau} ran to the grid edge in 2000/20002000/2000 draws under M1 and 1979/20001979/2000 under M2 (weight on level 5 at the edge: 0.480.48), so no depth estimate is quoted from the global fit; the reporting rule fixed in advance was to state this rather than to quote an edge value. What the fit identifies is the uplift: β=+14.3​[+13.2,+15.4]​pp\beta=+14.3~[+13.2,+15.4]\,\text{pp}, with wR2=0.58\text{wR}^{2}=0.58 (M2) against 0.100.10 (M1) and Δ​AICc=−12.6\Delta\text{AICc}=-12.6 in M2’s favor; the uplift explains 48% of weighted variance against 10% for the best cognitive-hierarchy component.

F.4 Pair-clustered sensitivity

Because the human corpus has pair structure the agent corpora lack, a sensitivity analysis outside the pre-registered specification clusters the human side by pair (9595 pairs; recorded seeds) in both the nearest-level bootstrap and the fit (weights and joint bootstrap). Every category keeps its most likely nearest-level answer, and 1515 rather than 1616 categories pass the 0.870.87 threshold; the fit keeps the original set. Every qualitative conclusion of the fit is unchanged: τ^\hat{\tau} remains at the grid edge, the uplift term remains warranted, and the uplift moves to +12.0​[+10.5,+13.3]​pp+12.0~[+10.5,+13.3]\,\text{pp} and explains 34%34\% of weighted variance (M1/M2 weighted R2R^{2} 0.410.41/0.740.74). The β\beta point value and the variance split therefore depend on the weighting, and are always quoted with this sensitivity alongside.

F.5 The post-hoc shared-cells fit

Restricting the pure mixture to the 44 categories where the two populations share a convention (those not above every level) yields an interior minimum at τ=4.27​[3.73,5.04]\tau=4.27~[3.73,5.04] (weighted R2=0.977R^{2}=0.977; probability of the grid edge 0.000.00; probability that τ\tau falls in the literature’s 11–33 range 0.000.00; weight on level 1 about 8%). This analysis is post-hoc: it was not in the pre-registered specification, rests on 44 categories, and no claim in the paper depends on it. It is reported because it makes clear what can be identified: depth can be estimated on the shared conventions and cannot be estimated off them.

F.6 What is and is not identified

Two questions must be kept apart. Which single level is a category nearest to? is answered by the nearest-level bootstrap (§F.2), category by category, and for 1616 of them the answer is “above all of them.” What mixture of levels best reproduces the human profile? is the parametric question, and its depth parameter is unidentified globally because these categories exceed the entire basis: no mixture of levels reaches them, so the fit pushes τ\tau to the grid edge and the flags fire. The identified content of the exercise is the decomposition, a shared component saturating by level 2–3 plus an uplift no level supplies, together with the caveats that the basis truncates at level 5 and that each level is trained with beliefs induced by a fixed base policy (uniformly random at level 1, the previous level’s policy above it). The levels are therefore not literal cognitive-hierarchy levels.

F.7 Depth is not what separates them: in full

Behavioral game theory finds that people use one to three steps of recursive reasoning about others [Stahl and Wilson, 1995, Nagel, 1995, Camerer et al., 2004], which appears to conflict with a human gap above every level of a five-level hierarchy. Looking category by category removes the conflict (Fig. 12).

On the three newest-card fresh-color categories (three of the 44 whose nearest level is 2 or 3), the agent profile saturates: level 2 already reaches +47 to +55 pp and levels 3–5 add almost nothing. Humans land at +51–+52 pp: at the level-2–3 value, and below the level-5 asymptote (P⁡(human<level 5)=P(\text{human}<\text{level 5})= 0.89–1.00).

Where humans diverge they are above every level (1616 of 2020 non-zero categories), which is the opposite pattern from limited recursion. Those categories split into two shapes: profiles still rising at level 5, and flat-low profiles, including both indirect-reference categories, that stay low at every level.

Neither side needs to recurse at the table. The agents’ recursion is performed during training and folded into a deployed policy that acts without search; taught human conventions may be a community’s reasoning compiled into lookup rules over years. The gap describes the product, how far play departs from the literal prediction, not the process. High human values therefore do not contradict kk-level limits, which concern on-the-fly reasoning in novel situations.

Appendix G Reproducibility

This appendix states how every number this paper computes can be regenerated.

Metric engine.

All posteriors are computed by the metric implementation released with the previous study [Fukushima et al., 2026], used at a pinned commit rather than as an installed package, so the joint posterior here is bit-identical to the previous study’s (verified play-for-play on the human corpus; Appendix E).

Replay verification.

Every game entering any analysis, generated or observational, is replayed in the metric engine and required to reproduce its ground-truth final score exactly before any statistic is computed. This holds for the self-play and mixed-level conditions (§2), the seed sweep (3500035000 games), every intervention condition and its baseline (Appendix D), the human corpus, the AH2AC2 release (1858/18581858/1858), and every clone evaluation (§H). No condition reported in this paper has a replay mismatch.

The audit pipeline.

The OBL ladder values (§2.2) are quoted as reported in the previous study [Fukushima et al., 2026]; this paper’s recomputation from the same games gives the same point values, and some interval ends differ by hundredths of a percentage point. Each analysis emits audited entries (value, interval, source artifact path, recomputation script, clustering and seed) into versioned JSON files; a generator turns those entries into the numbers the manuscript prints, and the build fails if any printed number lacks an audited entry. Every entry records the pipeline artifact it was recomputed from, so any value this paper computes can be traced to per-play records without consulting the manuscript itself.

Seed policy.

Environment seeds define disjoint blocks per condition; paired designs share their block with their baseline by construction. Analysis seeds (splits, bootstraps, fits) are recorded in the audit entries alongside draw counts. One documented exception to bit-level reproduction: the per-category bootstrap of §2.4 keys its seed on the Python hash of the category label, so those intervals reproduce only up to bootstrap error rather than bit-for-bit; every other interval this paper computes reproduces exactly from its recorded seed.

Release.

The analysis pipelines, the audit JSONs, the generated tables and figures, and the derived per-play records for the agent conditions will be released with the published version. The human and AH2AC2 corpora are redistributed only as derived, de-identified records consistent with their sources’ terms. Raw agent game logs stay on the generation server, because they derive from checkpoints licensed for non-commercial use; the included generation scripts regenerate them. The generation records name each checkpoint and environment seed but no code commit or checkpoint hash. The OBL commit and the hashes of all 2525 checkpoints used here were read from the generation server in October 2026 and describe the files at that time. On that server, the unmasked intervention code path regenerated the level-5 baseline action for action (1000/10001000/1000 games; Appendix D).

Appendix H Behavioral clones: does cloning preserve the human-specific cells?

Behavioral clones.

We trained clones of human play and of level-5 play identically, at matched data scale, with registered predictions. They reproduce the asymmetry of §3.1. The control clone preserves its source’s structure (r=0.967r=0.967 at scale). The human clone reaches level 5’s gap on the dominant shared convention (+59.9​[+58.0,+61.7]​pp+59.9~[+58.0,+61.7]\,\text{pp}), while indirect reference and the unhinted newest-card cell collapse to −5.7​[−21.6,+12.9]-5.7~[-21.6,+12.9] and −32.0​[−37.6,−24.4]​pp-32.0~[-37.6,-24.4]\,\text{pp} (the latter below literal chance). Aggregate similarity to humans is not fidelity on the channels where humans differ from machines.

The channels of §3.1 matter beyond this paper because the field increasingly evaluates coordination agents against behaviorally-cloned human proxies rather than people; AH2AC2’s own evaluation protocol rests on behavioral-cloning stand-ins for the community measured above [Dizdarević et al., 2025]. Cloning imitates the distribution of human actions; whether it also reproduces the human gaps on indirect reference and on unhinted cards is what our instrument can test.

Design.

We train a clone of human play (HC: the AH2AC2 open games, 1,7001{,}700 training / 158158 held out; the hanab.live corpus, the human reference below, is not used for training) and, as the control, a clone of level-5 self-play (OC). Both use identical architecture, hyperparameters, data size and training steps: the OBL codebase’s encoder and policy network, trained by supervised learning only, and one frozen configuration for every clone. If OC preserves its source’s convention structure while HC loses the human-specific cells, the loss is cell-specific rather than an artifact of data scale. An OC series at 18581858, 5,0005{,}000 and 20,00020{,}000 games calibrates what cloning captures at each scale. Four predictions were registered, with timestamps, before any training: the level-5 clone keeps its source’s profile and fresh-color gap; the human clone keeps the fresh-color conventions but not the indirect-reference and unhinted cells; preservation improves with data; and the human clone is less coherent in self-play than the level-5 clone. Clones are measured with the full ground-truth pipeline of §2: exact posteriors, replay verification, the frozen taxonomy. Because matched-scale clones are not coherent in self-play (HC: 100.0%100.0\% zero-score games; OC: 97.2%97.2\%), their channel numbers come from a frozen-partner variant (clone fixed in seat 0 against level 5, 500500 games, clone-side plays only, still fully ground-truthed).

Cloning works where the data are dense.

At 20,00020{,}000 games the level-5 clone reproduces its source: category-profile r=0.967r=0.967 against level 5, gap +21.22​[+20.87,+21.58]​pp+21.22~[+20.87,+21.58]\,\text{pp} (source: +21.68​[+21.34,+22.02]+21.68~[+21.34,+22.02]), fresh-color cells within a point of the original (+56.9​[+56.2,+57.6]+56.9~[+56.2,+57.6] vs +56.8​[+56.4,+57.2]​pp+56.8~[+56.4,+57.2]\,\text{pp}). Preservation is monotone in data (r=0.842/0.916/0.967r=0.842/0.916/0.967 across the series). The method, the architecture and the instrument are therefore all sufficient; what cloning captures is a question of what the data contain and how often.

The shared conventions transfer; the human-specific cells do not.

At matched scale, the human clone reaches level 5’s gap on the dominant shared convention: in the level-5 category for an immediate play after a fresh color hint on the newest card, it reads +59.9​[+58.0,+61.7]​pp+59.9~[+58.0,+61.7]\,\text{pp}, against level 5’s +56.8​[+56.4,+57.2]​pp+56.8~[+56.4,+57.2]\,\text{pp} for the same category. The cells that separate humans from the OBL hierarchy do not survive cloning: indirect reference reads −5.7​[−21.6,+12.9]-5.7~[-21.6,+12.9] (color; humans +61.3​[+54.4,+66.0]+61.3~[+54.4,+66.0]) and −8.1​[−19.0,+3.9]​pp-8.1~[-19.0,+3.9]\,\text{pp} (rank; humans +41.1​[+31.9,+48.8]+41.1~[+31.9,+48.8]), and the unhinted cells read −32.0​[−37.6,−24.4]-32.0~[-37.6,-24.4] and −17.6​[−24.5,−9.6]​pp-17.6~[-24.5,-9.6]\,\text{pp} against the humans’ +48.8​[+38.4,+55.6]+48.8~[+38.4,+55.6] and +43.2​[+31.1,+51.5]+43.2~[+31.1,+51.5]. Every interval excludes the human value by tens of points. The control rules out the generic explanation: at the same data and configuration, OC preserves its source’s structure (r=0.929r=0.929 with the frozen partner). What HC loses tracks how often a cell appears in training (each unhinted cell holds 0.70.7–1.1%1.1\% of AH2AC2 plays), not how large its gap is.

Unhinted plays invert.

On the frozen-partner runs, the clone’s unhinted newest-card plays are worse than literal chance (−32.0​[−37.6,−24.4]​pp-32.0~[-37.6,-24.4]\,\text{pp}; failure rate 95.5%95.5\%), as are level 1’s in self-play (−13.9​[−17.6,−9.9]​pp-13.9~[-17.6,-9.9]\,\text{pp}). The clone’s value rests on few plays. A negative value here is consistent with a partner whose hints favor playable cards: the cards it leaves untouched are then less likely to be playable than the literal observer assumes. The partner alone does not account for the human clone’s value: with the same partner, the matched-scale level-5 clone reads +2.6​[−11.2,+16.7]​pp+2.6~[-11.2,+16.7]\,\text{pp} on this cell. Cloning reproduces the act of playing an unhinted card, not the situations in which humans make that play; one reading is that imitating surface behavior without the representation behind it is costly rather than neutral.

Scope.

This measures plain behavioral cloning at open-split scale (1,7001{,}700–18,30018{,}300 games, default configuration, no reinforcement learning). The deployed AH2AC2 proxies, cloned from 147,621147{,}621 closed games and refined with regularized self-play, are not measured here. The scaling series warns against reading absence as impossibility: structure preservation improves with data, so channel survival at 10510^{5} games is not ruled out. These results suggest that the shared, frequent conventions and the rare channels respond to imitation differently, so a proxy that matches human play on the former can differ from humans on the channels where humans differ from machines. Aggregate similarity is not channel fidelity: the same dissociation, at the level of evaluation methodology, that §3.3 found at the level of the metric.
